inlines.text: 如何衡量不同智能体执行常规、真实网络安全任务的成功程度？

blocks.text: 许多公司已经在自己的开发和部署生态中使用智能体，而攻击者有时会利用成群的攻击型智能体同时攻击数千家公司。为了帮助防御方为这个新时代做好准备，我们需要一个能比较这些智能体能力的评分。正因如此重要，学术界和业界的实验室都开始着手研究如何衡量，并制定正确衡量的标准，所以这个话题既及时又日益相关。

blocks.text: 大多数公开的网络安全智能体基准测试回答的，并不是防御方所问的那个问题。选择题测验衡量的是模型知识，而非生产环境表现；由另一个模型评判 LLM 输出，衡量的是两者之间的一致性，而非成功与否。我们要回答的是：智能体能否执行一次真实的攻击。

blocks.text: 规模也很重要。近期许多网络安全基准测试的任务数不足 30 个。在 50% 的成功率下，30 个任务给出的 95% 置信区间约为 ±18 个百分点，因此一个比另一个高 15 分的智能体未必就更好。

blocks.text: 评估效果，而不是用 LLM 打分

inlines.text: 评估效果，而不是用 LLM 打分

blocks.text: 真实标注是评估的基础。用 LLM 作为评判者来打分一直是标准做法，但评判者并不直接衡量成功。它们有偏差（往往偏好第一个选项）、有随机性（每次运行结果不同）、昂贵且缓慢，而且要想在长期使用的基准测试中使用它们，必须先做校准和去偏。当你使用评判者时，你衡量的是某个 LLM 是否认为智能体成功了。这个差异是系统里内嵌的一笔债。

inlines.text: 真实标注是评估的基础。用 LLM 作为评判者来打分一直是标准做法，但评判者并不直接衡量成功。它们有偏差（往往偏好第一个选项）、有随机性（每次运行结果不同）、昂贵且缓慢，而且要想在长期使用的基准测试中使用它们，必须先做校准和去偏。当你使用评判者时，你衡量的是某个 LLM 是否认为智能体成功了。这个差异是系统里内嵌的一笔债。

blocks.text: 我们改用代码来评判。每道题都设计成会留下可核查的痕迹，或输出精确的结构化结果，智能体退出后由确定性的评分器检查。代码评分器成本低、可重复运行，也不是需要校准的模型。

blocks.text: 只要有机会，智能体就会走捷径：上网查答案、从磁盘上读现成解法，或者操纵评分器。如果分数是在能联网搜索、能查 CVE 数据库、文件夹里还写着题目名称的条件下拿到的，那衡量的就是别的东西了：究竟是完成了任务，还是攻破了任务。CTFusion 仅仅放宽了联网搜索权限，解题率就变化了多达 12 个百分点。

blocks.text: 构建基准测试是一项不简单、需要持续演进的工作，很容易在还没跑通端到端流程时就先写 300 道题。我们反过来采用精益创业的原则：先做出一个能手工检查的小规模端到端基线，再逐步迭代。

blocks.text: How do you measure the success with which different agents perform regular, real-world cybersecurity tasks?

inlines.text: How do you measure the success with which different agents perform regular, real-world cybersecurity tasks?

blocks.text: Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once. To help defenders prepare for this new era, we need a score that compares what these agents can do. Because of how important this is, labs in academia across the industry are starting to work on measuring it and setting a standard for how to do it correctly, so the topic is timely and increasingly relevant.

blocks.text: In this post I’ll share the key principles Wiz followed to tackle this benchmarking imperative in the relaunch of our Cyber Model Arena. The full methodology, how we graded, and gathered our tasks is available for download. As of the writing of this blog, the Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9 consists of 26 models, four general-purpose harnesses, 59 agents, 327 challenges, three attempts per challenge, and 1,000 seconds each (these numbers are constantly growing).

Measure success directly and deterministically, and apply anti-cheat measures: isolate the agent from the server and the internet, and give it no way to look up answers. Do not rely on an LLM-as-a-judge unless it is well designed, calibrated and free of bias.

LLM judges, small samples, task imbalance, model-only evaluation and answer leakage each make a benchmark unreliable. And start small: one harness, a quick and cheap model, a few tasks and a simple grader. Scale only after it works.

blocks.text: Most public cyber-agent benchmarks answer a different question than the one a defender is asking. A multiple-choice quiz benchmark measures model knowledge not production performance, and an LLM output judged by another model measures agreement between the two, not success. We aim to answer whether the agent can perform a real attack.

To reduce many competing metrics to a single number, pick one optimizing metric and treat everything else as a satisficing constraint. If you have five competing metrics and no way to reduce them, which agent is better becomes a debate over the metrics.

blocks.text: A benchmark can only speak for the tasks it contains. Sample only the hard tasks and you are no longer measuring success on the job, you are measuring success on hard tasks. And a benchmark that claims to measure "offensive capability" from a single task category oversells itself.

blocks.text: Size matters too. Many recent cybersecurity benchmarks have fewer than 30 tasks. At a 50% success rate, 30 tasks give a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±18 points, so an agent that scores 15 points higher than another is not necessarily better.

blocks.text: Grade an effect, not with LLMs

inlines.text: Grade an effect, not with LLMs

blocks.text: Ground truth is the foundation of evaluation. It has been standard practice to grade with an LLM-as-a-Judge, but judges do not directly measure success. They are biased (they often prefer the first option), random (they give different results each run), expensive, and slow, and they must be calibrated and de-biased before you can use them in a long-lived benchmark. When you use a judge, you measure whether an LLM thinks the agent succeeded. That difference is a debt baked into the system.

When you use a judge, you measure whether an LLM thinks the agent succeeded. That difference is a debt baked into the system.

blocks.text: We use code instead. Every challenge is designed to leave a checkable effect behind or report precise structured outputs, and a deterministic grader inspects it after the agent is gone. Code graders are cheap, re-runnable, and not a model you have to calibrate.

blocks.text: Agents will shortcut a task when they can. They look the answer up online, read a solution off disk, or manipulate the grader. A score collected with web search, a CVE database or the challenge name in the folder measures something else: success at the task or success at breaking it. CTFusion moved their solve rate by as much as 12 points just by raising web-search access.

blocks.text: Building a benchmark is a nontrivial, evolving effort, and it is tempting to write 300 challenges before anything runs end to end. We apply lean-startup rules instead: get a small end-to-end baseline you can inspect by hand, then iterate.

blocks.text: Give an agent more time and money and it will usually solve more. So the useful chart plots success against what a solve costs. Any agent off the Pareto frontier is strictly worse than one on it. For example, Claude Code with GPT-5.6 Sol averages 64.2% pass@1 at $8.29 and 27.2 minutes per solve, however the Pareto frontier Codex + GPT-6 Luna is strictly better, averaging 64.5% pass@1 at only $0.05 and 6.3 minutes per solve.

A semantically correct root cause that misses the expected symbol scores 0. We chose precision over recall.
websec.fr is a known corpus. Isolation stops the agent from looking up the answer, not from remembering it from training (possibly resulting in benchmark contamination).
1,000 seconds is enough for most successful attacks we observed. In the future we think it is better to limit cost than time.

blocks.text: Our Cyber Model Arena shows how different agents perform on common cybersecurity tasks, across 327 isolated challenges in four categories. To build an agentic cybersecurity benchmark, fix the why, the what and the how first, and define the agent, the task mix, the grader, the isolation, the budget and the attempts. Get one wrong and the benchmark becomes garbage in, garbage out.
